title: Common Phone Scams Targeting Seniors and How to Respond
bigPicture: Most phone scams work the same way: they rush you, ask for money or personal information, and want payment that is hard to trace. Slow down, hang up, and check with a number you already know.
whatYouNeedToKnow: Government impersonation: government agencies will never call, email, text, or message you on social media to ask for money or personal information. Scammers may threaten arrest or benefit suspension.
Tech support: legitimate tech companies will not contact you by phone, email, or text to say your computer has a problem. Real security pop-ups never ask you to call a phone number.
Prizes and lotteries: real prizes are free. If you must pay fees, taxes, or shipping to get a prize, it is a scam.
Family emergency: a caller claims to be a relative in trouble and presses you to send money fast. Some use AI to copy a loved one's voice.
Scammers ask for wire transfers, gift cards, cryptocurrency, or payment apps because these are hard to trace and hard to get back.
Caller ID can be faked, so do not trust it.
commonMistakesToAvoid: Paying or sharing personal information because a caller sounds official or urgent.
Calling back the number the caller gave you instead of one you know is correct.
Pressing numbers on a robocall, or clicking links in unexpected messages.
Giving a bank account number, card number, or Social Security number to claim a prize.
actionSteps: Hang up or ignore the contact.
Contact the real agency or company using a number you already know is correct. For Medicare, call 1-800-MEDICARE.
Talk to a family member or friend before you send any money.
If you paid or shared information, act as quickly as you can and contact the company you paid through.
Report scams at ReportFraud.ftc.gov and to your state attorney general.
